title: Engaged and Exhausted: Why Your Filipino Employees Are a Hidden Flight Risk
summary: Filipino employees are the most engaged in Southeast Asia and the most stressed. Why that mix is a retention risk, and what HR can do.
body_markdown:
If you run a workforce in the Philippines, your engagement scores probably look good. They shouldn't reassure you.


Gallup's State of the Global Workplace 2026 report found that 39% of Filipino employees are engaged at work, the highest in Southeast Asia and nearly double the global average of 20%. The same report found that 50% of Filipino employees experienced stress for much of the previous day. That's double the Southeast Asian average and 10 points above the global figure.


Your people are committed. They are also running hot. And in a job market as open as the Philippines, that combination is how you lose your best people.


## Two numbers that shouldn't sit together, but do


The Philippines stands out on almost every measure Gallup tracks, in both directions:

Daily stress has also risen three points against the previous three-year average. This isn't a blip.


Local data tells the same story. Jobstreet's Workplace Happiness Index for the Philippines found 77% of employees describe themselves as happy at work. Yet only 41% said they feel in control of their stress, and 38% said they feel burned out or extremely exhausted because of work.


Gallup's own consultants put it simply: commitment and strain can exist in the same person at the same time. Most engagement programmes are only built to measure the first.


## Engagement is not the same as sustainability


Engaged employees give discretionary effort. They stay late, cover for colleagues, and take on the extra project. In a healthy environment, that's what makes teams great. In an overstretched one, it's what burns people out.


An engagement score tells you how committed someone is today. It doesn't tell you how long they can keep it up. When a company celebrates a high score without asking about workload, it often ends up rewarding the very behaviour that leads to exhaustion.


## Why the job market makes this urgent


Three in four Filipino employees told Gallup it's a good time to find a job, well above Indonesia at 64% and Singapore at 42%. That changes the maths of burnout.


In a tight market, an exhausted employee grits their teeth and stays. In an open one, they update their profile. And the people most likely to leave are not your disengaged employees. They're the engaged high performers carrying the heaviest load, who are also the easiest for competitors to hire.


## Signs you might be missing it


- Your most engaged teams are also the ones working the longest hours.
- High performers are taking on more, while their managers report everything is fine.
- Exit interviews mention workload or burnout from people who scored as engaged a few months earlier.
- New joiners say they feel overwhelmed within their first 90 days.
- Leave balances are piling up because people feel they can't step away.


## What HR leaders in the Philippines can do


**1. Measure strain alongside engagement.** Add questions on workload, recovery and stress to every listening touchpoint. A high engagement score paired with high strain is a warning, not a win.


**2. Watch your most engaged people most closely.** They're the ones least likely to complain and most likely to be poached. Check in with them regularly, not just when something breaks.


**3. Ask in the language people actually use.** Many employees express themselves more honestly in Filipino or Taglish than in formal English. In inFeedo's experience, switching to local languages can lift response rates by around 10%.


**4. Hold managers accountable for workload, not just output.** Give managers visibility of which team members are stretched, and make redistributing work part of their job.


**5. Follow up fast on negative signals.** When someone says they're exhausted, a reply weeks later is too late. Speed of response is what tells employees their feedback was worth giving.


## The bottom line


The Philippines has something most countries would envy: a workforce that genuinely cares about its work. The risk is treating that commitment as unlimited. Organisations that measure strain as carefully as they measure engagement will keep their best people. The rest will keep wondering why their top performers resigned.
